name: Dunk
seoDesc: Dunk: work out minimum vertical leap from the standing reach and the jumping energy. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Dunk calculator the standing reach, the jumping energy, the initial jumping speed and the palm size and it returns minimum vertical leap. It is built for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Dunk calculator work?
sections.html:
The Dunk calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports minimum vertical leap in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the hoop type); then you type in the standing reach, the jumping energy, the initial jumping speed and the palm size.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as 2nd grade or below, 3rd to 4ᵗʰ grade and 5th to 6th grade. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in joules. The unit chip switches it to any of the 33 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Dunk calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Minimum vertical leap=hoop height + palm size − standing reach
Minimum vertical leap=(1 ÷ 2) × (initial jumping speed ^ 2) ÷ gravitational acceleration
Minimum vertical leap=jumping energy ÷ (body mass × gravitational acceleration)
Hang time=2 × the square root of (2) × the square root of (minimum vertical leap ÷ gravitational acceleration)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in gravitational acc. on Earth, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Shown in seconds, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Acceleration, opening in gravitational acc. on Earth

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Dunk calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the standing reach, the jumping energy and the initial jumping speed — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Dunk calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns minimum vertical leap, derived from the standing reach, the jumping energy and the initial jumping speed. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Dunk calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the standing reach, the jumping energy, the initial jumping speed and the palm size, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter hoop height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Hoop height opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Hoop height = 0 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Dunk calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
